1.pericope_label: Wherefore laying aside all malice, and all guile... As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word

schools.summary: Ellicott alone gives the 'wherefore' a concrete history, reading the vices as a party quarrel — 'ill will put into action... on the part of these Hebrew Christians against their Gentile brethren' — and sorting them by function: 'the first plots, the second pretends not to plot, and the third rejoices to think of the plot succeeding.' On the babes he insists on 'newly, lately born, not born anew', the name fitting because 'they are still so far from maturity in Christ, as these sins testified'; he rejects the English 'of the word' as one that 'cannot possibly be right'; he would render the last clause 'ye tasted', looking back to the first conversion, 'when the taste of spiritual things is the most delicious. How sad to be past the relish for evangelical truth!'; and he disowns 'gracious' as adopted 'to suit the Prayer Book version of the Psalm'. His doctrinal point is that Peter applies to Christ a passage 'which otherwise we might not have thought of applying to Him in particular'. Barnes reads the milk-adjective as 'properly rational, pertaining to reason'; Robertson declines to choose between cleansing and undressing for the opening verb, notes that hypocrisies is singular 'in the best MSS' and the fourth word envies 'not murders, as B has it', and lays the two senses of the adjective side by side, giving the other its edge: unadulterated milk 'which, alas, is so hard to get'.

Gill has the vices for 'old worn out clothes, as filthy rags... never used more'. Calvin takes the connective back to the new birth — 'it is not sufficient for us to have been once called by the Lord, except we live as new creatures' — and pairs the two adjectives of the milk deliberately, since 'simplicity and quickness of understanding are two things apparently opposite; but they ought to be mixed together, lest simplicity should become insipid, and lest malicious craftiness should creep in.'

Clarke hears a rabbinic register, learning the law being called sucking and disciples 'those that suck the breast', argues for adding 'unto salvation' at the verse's end on ABC 'and about forty others' as 'undoubtedly genuine, and is very important', and reports that many manuscripts and several fathers read 'Christ' for 'gracious', 'from the similarity of the letters'. Wesley adds that dissimulation 'is the outward expression of guile in the heart', and reads the conditional as a statement.

Henry narrows malice to 'settled overgrown anger, retained till it inflames a man to design mischief', and splits hypocrisy by sphere: 'in matters of religion hypocrisy is counterfeit piety. In civil conversation hypocrisy is counterfeit friendship.'

debates.question: What does the adjective rendered 'of the word' mean?

positions.view: Milk made up of the word, the two adjectives paired so that simplicity and understanding are mixed together.
'Properly rational, pertaining to reason' — the elementary truths of the gospel adapted to babes.
The English 'of the word' 'cannot possibly be right'.
Both readings stand side by side, undecided.

debates.question: Is the text of these verses secure?

positions.view: No: 'unto salvation' should be added at the end of verse 2 on ABC 'and about forty others', and many manuscripts read 'Christ' for 'gracious' in verse 3, 'from the similarity of the letters'.
Only small corrections: hypocrisies is singular 'in the best MSS', and the fourth vice is envies, 'not murders, as B has it'.

outliers.view: Reads the list of vices as a specific quarrel between Hebrew Christians and their Gentile brethren rather than as generic sins.
Makes the textual case for 'unto salvation' at the end of verse 2, calling the addition 'undoubtedly genuine, and is very important'.

themes: Wherefore laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings,
As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:
If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious.

4.pericope_label: To whom coming, as unto a living stone, disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious

schools.summary: Robertson finds 'an apparent intentional contradiction between living and stone', of a piece with the living hope and living word earlier, and supplies the words that carry the contrast: the verb for rejection means 'to repudiate after test', the balancing phrase is spatial, 'by the side of God, as he looks at it', and the adjective is not the proved one that test-word leads you to expect but precious, 'a pre-eminence of position with' God. Barnes admits the difficulty of 'living stone' rather than resolving it, the phrase being 'unusual, and is not found, I think, except in this place', the point being 'a temple composed of living materials', redeemed men. Ellicott registers the shift from regeneration imagery to temple imagery, insists that 'the very structure and order of the sentence puts Jesus Christ first. Foundation first, building afterwards', objects that 'it is a pity to insert as unto with our version', and denies that Peter had his own surname in mind.

Gill denies that the coming is conversion: it 'does not design the first act of faith on Christ, or a soul's first coming to Christ, but an after and continued exercise of faith on him'; and he takes the verse as a disclaimer, Peter showing 'that he is not the rock, but Christ is the rock on which the church is built'. Calvin makes the coming the effect of the taste just mentioned, since 'the human mind necessarily dreads and shuns God, as long as it regards him as rigid and severe', and answers the offence of the world's rejection by saying that Christ 'notwithstanding, retains his own worth and honor before God'.

Clarke translates the adjective 'honourable' and extends the honour to the building, since those united to him 'partake of the same honor' — the stones being 'of no use but as they occupy their proper places' — and draws the assurance: 'God can never be mistaken in his choice; therefore he that chooses Christ for his portion shall never be confounded.' Wesley extends the list of rejecters past the obvious, not only 'Jews, Turks, heathens, infidels; but by all Christians, so called, who live in sin, or who hope to be saved by their own works'.

Henry hears the metaphor as its first readers would: to 'a capricious wit, or an infidel, this description may seem rough and harsh', but to Jews 'who placed much of their religion in their magnificent temple, and who understood the prophetical style', it 'would appear very elegant and proper'.

debates.question: Is Peter alluding to his own name?

positions.view: Yes, and as a disclaimer: he 'shows that he is not the rock, but Christ is the rock on which the church is built'.

'More than doubtful.' The word here is neither petros nor petra but lithos, and neither of the first two 'could possibly be used of the squared wrought stone', both meaning the native unhewn substratum.

debates.question: What is 'coming' to Christ?

positions.view: Not conversion but 'an after and continued exercise of faith on him'.
The effect of having tasted his goodness, so that men 'forget themselves and hasten to him'.
The participle is the verb behind 'proselyte': 'joining Him therefore as proselytes.'

outliers.view: Lets the difficulty stand rather than resolving it: 'there seems to be an incongruity in it, in attributing life to a stone.'
Counts among the rejecters not only unbelievers but 'all Christians, so called, who live in sin, or who hope to be saved by their own works'.

themes: To whom coming, as unto a living stone, disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious,

5.pericope_label: Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house... Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone

schools.summary: Barnes says 'lively' should have been rendered 'living', since the modern word denotes 'active, quick, sprightly'. Ellicott calls the variation 'arbitrary, the Greek being precisely the same', prefers the imperative reading of the verb as suiting 'the hortatory character of the whole Epistle', says the temple is regarded 'not in its capacity of a place for worship so much as a place for Divine inhabitation', corrects the introduction of the quotation to 'because' rather than 'wherefore also', and reports the exegetical history in which the early Jewish reading referred Isaiah's stone to the Messiah while 'the later Rabbinical expositors, probably by way of opposition to the Christians, explained it to mean Hezekiah'. Robertson reads the corporate sense out of the verb Jesus used to Peter, concluding that Peter understood that saying 'to be not a local church, but the church general', says plainly that Peter holds 'all believers are priests and can approach God directly', and notes that the term for chief corner stone was 'apparently invented by Isaiah'.

Gill notes the metaphor was not Peter's invention, poets having called stones 'living' while they lay in the quarry, and makes his own use of it sharper: saints 'lie in the same quarry, and are the same by nature as the rest of mankind, till dug out and separated from thence by the powerful and efficacious grace of God'; on the quotation he observes that the Targum applies it to a mighty king without naming him, 'but Jarchi expressly names him'. Calvin finds the verb's mood ambiguous but the exhortation unaffected, and insists the house is one: 'though every one of us is said to be the temple of God, yet all are united together in one, and must be joined together by mutual love, so that one temple may be made of us all.'

Clarke faces the objection nobody else raises — 'what analogy is there between the stones of a building and a multitude of human beings?' — and answers philologically, since in Hebrew the words for house, son, daughter and stone all stand on one root meaning 'he built'. He locates the corner stone at the angle 'where its two sides form the ground work of a side and end wall', inferring that in Jesus 'both Jews and Gentiles were to be united', and turns the Hebrew of the closing promise into consolation: the believer 'need not haste to flee away, for no enemy shall ever be able to annoy him'. Wesley adds two words to it: 'in time or in eternity.'

debates.question: Is the verb an indicative or an imperative?

positions.view: Undecidable — 'the termination in Greek is ambiguous' — but either way Peter 'meant to exhort the faithful to consecrate themselves as a spiritual temple to God'.
'The one is as grammatical as the other', but the imperative suits 'the hortatory character of the whole Epistle'.

debates.question: How is the church like a building of stones?

positions.view: By philology: in Hebrew house, son, daughter and stone share the root meaning 'he built', so the analogy is in the language before it is in the figure.
By mutual love, all fitted together so that 'one temple may be made of us all'.
By the verb Jesus used to Peter, which shows the metaphor means 'not a local church, but the church general'.

outliers.view: Derives the whole metaphor from a Hebrew root shared by the words for house, son, daughter and stone.
Points out that classical poets already called quarry stones 'living', citing Virgil's vivoque sedilia saxo.

themes: Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.
Wherefore also it is contained in the scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded.

7.pericope_label: Unto you therefore which believe he is precious... the same is made the head of the corner

schools.summary: Barnes defends the Authorised text against its own margin: it is true that believing on Christ is an honour, 'but it is very doubtful whether this is the idea of Peter', since 'the apostle was not showing that it was an honour to believe on Christ, but was stating the estimate which was put on him by those who believe'. He argues the point from evidence rather than definition, Christians perceiving 'a value in him which is seen in nothing else' and avowing him 'their best friend'. Ellicott takes the other side, resting on the contrast, since both Hebrew and Greek 'may with equal propriety be translated honoured, and this contrasts better with the shame just spoken of'; he adds the textual note that 'the better reading is, Unto them which disbelieve', and notices that Peter 'stops short, and inserts (by a quotation) the historical fact which brought the shame'. Robertson glosses the noun as 'the preciousness' or 'the honour', and traces the psalm through its uses: Jesus quoted it against the Sanhedrin, Peter at the Beautiful Gate, and 'here he quotes it again to the same purpose'.

Gill spends his space on who the believers are not: not 'all they that can say their creed, or give their assent to the articles of it'; not all who believe a divine revelation; not all who believe the whole Gospel and every truth in it; nor 'all that say they believe, or profess to do so' — but only those 'who have seen themselves lost and undone by sin, their need of a Saviour'. Calvin reaches the inference by a shorter road — 'Christ is a precious stone in the sight of God; then he is such to the faithful' — because 'it is faith alone which reveals to us the value and excellency of Christ', and draws out the two things the verse asserts, that Christ 'was rejected by those who bore rule in the Church of God' and that 'their efforts were all in vain'.

Clarke renders it 'the honor is to you who believe', meaning 'the honor of being in this building, and of having your souls saved through the blood of the Lamb', and lets the rejected keep the stone: 'that very person whom they reject is head of the corner — is Lord over all, and has all power in the heavens and the earth.' Wesley makes the same point prospectively, that unbelievers 'too will at length find him such to their sorrow'.

debates.question: Does the verse say Christ is precious, or that the honour belongs to believers?

positions.view: Christ is precious. The margin's 'an honour' is true in itself, 'but it is very doubtful whether this is the idea of Peter', and 'the connexion demands this interpretation'.
The honour belongs to the believers, contrasting with the shame just promised: 'unto you therefore, the believers, belongs the honour.'

outliers.view: Defines faith almost entirely by exclusion, ruling out creed-reciting, assent to revelation, assent to the whole Gospel, and profession alike.
Notices that Peter breaks off instead of stating the unbelievers' shame, substituting the historical fact of the rejection.

themes: Unto you therefore which believe he is precious: but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner,

8.pericope_label: And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence... whereunto also they were appointed

schools.summary: Ellicott insists the figure changes completely — 'there is no thought whatever of the stone as a material for building; the thought is that of a mass of rock on the road, on which the terror-stricken fugitives stumble and fall' — and reads it out of Isaiah's Immanuel section, where the stone is 'such a sanctuary as that of Bethel, a consecrated stone to which a man might flee as an asylum' but becomes 'a vexatious and dangerous obstacle' to those who do not trust it. He accuses the Septuagint of guile in 'deliberately inserting the word not twice over', reverses the apparent Pauline dependence, and rearranges the words of the last clause so that the participle explains the verb. Robertson distinguishes the two nouns — one 'an obstacle against which one strikes by accident', the other 'a trap set to trip one, but both make one fall' — and quotes Bigg on the appointment: 'their disobedience is not ordained, the penalty of their disobedience is.' Barnes takes the second word back to its origin, 'a trap-stick — a crooked stick on which the bait is fastened, which the animal strikes against, and so springs the trap'.

Gill catalogues the offences that made men stumble — the virgin birth, the meanness of Christ's parents, the education that made them ask 'how he should know letters', and 'the obscurity of his kingdom'. Calvin keeps the fault off Christ, whose 'proper office is to prepare us for a spiritual temple to God; but it is the fault of men that they stumble at him', so that 'it is as it were an accidental thing that he becomes a rock of offense'; he turns the charge on his own age — 'the Papists do the same in the present day; they worship only the name of Christ, while they cannot endure the doctrine of the Gospel' — and lays out both senses of the appointment, inclining to the harder.

Clarke names a single cause for the rejection, and not the usual one: the Gospel 'called the Gentiles to be a peculiar people whom the Jews believed to be everlastingly reprobated', which was 'the true cause why the Jews rejected the Gospel'. He escapes the difficulty of the last clause by re-punctuating, carrying the sense forward from the preceding verse on Macknight's authority. Wesley states the appointment hardest: 'God having appointed from all eternity, he that believeth not shall be damned.'

debates.question: To what were they appointed?

positions.view: Both senses are possible — appointed to believe, since 'the promise of salvation was destined for them', or 'appointed to unbelief; as Pharaoh is said to have been set up for this end' — and he inclines to the second on the strength of a particle, taking the antecedent to be the stumbling.
Only to the penalty: 'their disobedience is not ordained, the penalty of their disobedience is.'
Prophetically rather than causally: the Old Testament prophecies 'marked them for such a destiny', it being 'no unforeseen, accidental consequence of the gospel'.
From eternity, on the condition of unbelief: 'he that believeth not shall be damned.'
Not to stumbling at all: re-punctuate so that 'the disobedient stumble against the word, or doctrine, to which verily they were appointed'.

debates.question: Why did the Jews reject the Gospel?

positions.view: Because of the circumstances of Christ's birth, parentage, education and poverty, and 'the obscurity of his kingdom'.
Because it 'called the Gentiles to be a peculiar people whom the Jews believed to be everlastingly reprobated'.

outliers.view: Charges the Septuagint translators with guile, having inserted a negative twice over 'in its endeavour to make out the best possible case for Israel', and argues Peter's pairing of the quotations goes back to Christ rather than to Paul.
Applies the stumbling to sixteenth-century Rome: 'they worship only the name of Christ, while they cannot endure the doctrine of the Gospel.'

themes: And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient: whereunto also they were appointed.

9.pericope_label: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people

schools.summary: Ellicott presses the first title into a doctrine of the church — the readers are not 'individuals selected one by one and left in isolation, but a tribe consolidated' — and is precise about 'royal', which 'does not seem intended to imply that every Christian is a king' but 'describes his belonging to the King as we might speak of the royal apartments, the royal borough, or even of the royal servants'. He renders the fourth title 'a people for a special reservation', notes the words 'describe the whole Israelite nation as they stood beneath Mount Sinai', and draws the consequence that 'the sacerdotal office was as common to all Israelites under the Law as it is to all the new Israel under the Gospel'. Barnes prefers Doddridge's reading, that they 'at once bore the dignity of kings, and the sanctity of priests', and treats Peter's use of Hosea as 'a mere allusion'. Robertson defends the old English — 'the old rendering, a peculiar people, had this idea of possession' — calls the noun for praises an 'old word for any preeminence (moral, intellectual, military)', and states church order flatly: the officer is presbyter-overseer, not priest; 'we are all priests.'

Gill takes the kinship three ways: akin to God as Father, to Christ as head and brother, and to one another as one household. Calvin turns the borrowed titles into a warning — 'Moses called formerly your fathers a holy nation, a priestly kingdom, and God's peculiar people: all these high titles do now far more justly belong to you; therefore you ought to beware lest your unbelief should rob you of them' — and reads verse 10 of the Jews first, scattered 'as the torn members of a body'.

Clarke sets the titles out from Deuteronomy and Exodus, observing that what was 'formerly given to the whole Jewish Church... are here given to Christians in general in the same way', and says the readers 'had been Gentiles, covered with ignorance and superstition'. Wesley splits the tenth verse down the middle: 'the former part... particularly respects the gentiles; the latter, the Jews.'

debates.question: Who were the people who 'in time past were not a people'?

positions.view: Gentiles, 'covered with ignorance and superstition', now brought in by the Gospel.
Mainly those 'who had been Gentiles, and who had never been recognised as the people of God', Hosea being used only by allusion.
Both, one in each half of the verse.
The Jews first, scattered and repudiated, with Paul extending the same prophecy to the Gentiles 'not without reason'.
Not proof of a Gentile readership at all — 'such, however, is by no means the case; in fact, the opposite' — the unpitied in Hosea being Israel itself.

debates.question: What follows from 'a royal priesthood' for Christian ministry?

positions.view: That priesthood belongs to all: 'the sacerdotal office was as common to all Israelites under the Law as it is to all the new Israel under the Gospel', and the officer in Christian churches is presbyter-overseer, not priest.

outliers.view: Denies that 'royal' means every Christian is a king, reading it as belonging to the King, 'as we might speak of the royal apartments, the royal borough'.
Treats Peter's Hosea quotation as borrowed language rather than shared reference, 'without meaning to say that both refer to the same subject'.

themes: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God: which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.

11.pericope_label: Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts

schools.summary: Ellicott disowns the English 'pilgrim', which "does not originally, or in this place, mean one on a pilgrimage. It implies no journeying, but simply residence in a foreign country", takes the words as metaphorical rather than literal, traces them to the psalm where they "prepare for the description of distress which is to follow", and finds the adjective rendered 'honest' untranslatable: "we have no word adequate to represent this charming adjective", it being "the ordinary Greek word for beautiful, and implies the attractiveness of the sight". On the disputed conjunction he prefers the margin and finds a use for the slander itself. Barnes defines the two nouns the other way — 'one who travels to a distance from his own country to visit a holy place... then a traveller, a wanderer' — and lays out the two constructions of 'whereas' without arbitrating, since 'the question which is meant is not very important'. Robertson keeps the lusts narrow, 'the grosser sins of the flesh', puts the Gentile scrutiny as surveillance — 'the Gentiles are on the watch for slips in moral conduct by the Christians' — and hears a 'clear echo' of the Sermon on the Mount in the last clause.

Gill hears the tone in the grammar: Peter does not 'in an authoritative way command, as he might have done, as an apostle, but, as a friend, he entreats'. Calvin denies the words are literal — the children of God 'wherever they may be, are only guests in this world' — widens the fleshly lusts past 'those gross concupiscences which we have in common with animals, as the Sophists hold' to 'all those sinful passions and affections of the soul', finds neither 'conversation' nor 'honest' suitable English, and explains the urgency historically: the Jews 'were not only hated everywhere, but were also almost abhorred'.

Clarke takes the two words at face value, these being 'strangers and pilgrims in the most literal sense of the word', scattered through Asia and Pontus; makes the lusts 'marshalled and drawn up in battle array, to fight against the soul; either to slay it, or to bring it into captivity'; observes that in the first age 'the Christians and the Jews were confounded together' abroad, so Christians 'shared in their blame'; and reads the day of visitation as judgment on the disobedient Jews. Wesley splits the two words by scale — 'the first word properly means, those who are in a strange house; the second, those who are in a strange country' — and reads the day of visitation as mercy: 'the time when he shall give them fresh offers of his mercy.'

Henry adds the uncomfortable inference that 'even the best of men... need to be exhorted to keep from the worst sins', and keeps the day of visitation open, a day 'wherein God may call to repentance by his word and his grace'.

debates.question: Are 'strangers and pilgrims' literal or figurative?

positions.view: Literal: they were actually dispersed through Asia and Pontus.
Figurative here, whatever the earlier use in the letter: the children of God 'wherever they may be, are only guests in this world'.

debates.question: What is the day of visitation?

positions.view: Judgment — 'when God should come to execute judgment on the disobedient Jews, in the destruction of their civil polity'.
Mercy — 'the time when he shall give them fresh offers of his mercy'.
Either, a day 'wherein God may call to repentance by his word and his grace'.

debates.question: How wide are the 'fleshly lusts'?

positions.view: Narrow: 'the grosser sins of the flesh.'
Wide: not only what we share with animals but 'all those sinful passions and affections of the soul'.

outliers.view: Finds a positive use for the slander: 'the very fact of the heathen having slandered them will make their testimony in the day of visitation all the more striking', as Thomas's doubts tend to the confirmation of the faith.
Explains the pressure historically, Christians abroad being confounded with Jews and sharing their unpopularity.

themes: Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;
Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation.

13.pericope_label: Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake: whether it be to the king, as supreme

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the verse against its Pauline model and finds the reasoning reversed: in Romans the ground is that 'the authority proceeds from God Himself', but here they submit 'because of the practical consequences of not submitting' — for the Lord's sake, 'in order not to bring discredit upon His teaching, and persecution upon His Church'. He explains the difference by circumstance, Peter writing because 'ignorant and foolish men' were misrepresenting the Church 'as a kind of Internationalist or Socialist conspiracy'; warns that Peter 'does not say we are to submit to every law that men may pass'; notes that 'the name king, though detested in Latin, was used without scruple by the provincial Greeks'; insists 'the person by whom they are here said to be sent is Cæsar, not the Lord'; and illustrates how personal imperial government was from Pliny's correspondence. Robertson says Peter 'approves no special kind of government, but he supports law and order' unless it 'steps in between God and man', and holds the governors sent 'by God, as Jesus made plain to Pilate'. Barnes enters the usual limitation, that what is ordained be 'not contrary to the law of God', reads 'king' generally, and quotes Ulpian on a president's duty.

Gill takes the human creature to be the heathen magistrate, created and installed as such. Calvin gets a doctrine of society out of the verb, which means to construct a building: 'God the maker of the world has not left the human race in a state of confusion, that they might live after the manner of beasts, but as it were in a building regularly formed' — the arrangement called human 'not because it has been invented by man, but because a mode of living, well arranged and duly ordered, is peculiar to men'. He adds the period detail that the Jews were 'counted infamous... because they were regarded on account of their perverseness as ungovernable', and concludes there is 'no kind of government to which we ought not to submit'.

Clarke says the words 'literally signify, not every ordinance of man, but every human creature', but since the verb can also mean to arrange, 'it is better to understand the words thus, All the constituted authorities'. He alone allows no practical reservation: 'genuine Christians have nothing to do with the laws but to obey them. Society and civil security are in a most dangerous state when the people take it into their heads that they have a right to remodel and change the laws.' Wesley keeps both grounds in a line: 'instrumentally these are ordained by men; but originally all their power is from God.'

Henry draws the distinction that softens the question: magistracy 'is certainly of divine right; but the particular form of government, the power of the magistrate, and the persons who are to execute this power, are of human institution'.

debates.question: Why should Christians submit?

positions.view: Not because the authority comes from God, as in Romans, but 'because of the practical consequences of not submitting' — to avoid discredit and persecution for the Church.
Because the power is God's however it is conveyed: 'instrumentally these are ordained by men; but originally all their power is from God.'

debates.question: Are there limits to the submission?

positions.view: Yes: what is ordained must be 'not contrary to the law of God'; Peter 'does not say we are to submit to every law that men may pass', and supports order only until it 'steps in between God and man'.
Not in practice: 'genuine Christians have nothing to do with the laws but to obey them', and reform movements put civil security 'in a most dangerous state'.

debates.question: By whom are the governors sent?

positions.view: By Cæsar: 'the person by whom they are here said to be sent is Cæsar, not the Lord.'
By God, 'as Jesus made plain to Pilate', who received his authority from above.

outliers.view: The only voice to deny any practical right of reform, holding that popular attempts to 'remodel and change the laws' endanger civil security.
Reads the letter's setting through the charge that the Church was a subversive organisation — 'a kind of Internationalist or Socialist conspiracy'.

themes: Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake: whether it be to the king, as supreme;
Or unto governors, as unto them that are sent by him for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well.

15.pericope_label: For so is the will of God, that with well doing ye may put to silence the ignorance of foolish men

schools.summary: Ellicott finds contempt everywhere in the clause — the muzzling implies 'there is something of the animal about these foolish men', and even 'men' 'might be rendered people or creatures'; reads 'as free' as the gist of the accusation, since the Christian 'professed himself in a certain sense to be above the laws', a position 'the heathen state resented'; and takes 'honour all men' as an advance on Paul, who said the honour was for those to whom it was due, where Peter 'says that this includes all men; there is not one who can be entirely despised, not one who has quite lost the likeness of Christ'. He also quotes Leighton on the arrangement of the four commands, the fear of God 'set in the middle betwixt these, as the common spring of all duty to men'. Barnes reads the accusers as foolish 'in the sense of evil-disposed, or wicked', yet holds that 'though there might be malice at the bottom, the charges were really based on ignorance', notes that the Jews 'never willingly acknowledged their subjection to any other power', and limits the honour to what is 'due to them according to their personal worth, and to the rank and office which they sustain'. Robertson notes the alliteration, qualifies the command — 'not with the same honour' — and makes the point negatively: 'there is no such thing as absolute freedom... for that is anarchy.'

Gill keeps the freedom real but bounded: they were 'Christ's freemen, free from sin... but then they were not free to sin'. Calvin admits the phrase 'to stop up ignorance' 'may seem harsh on account of its novelty' but keeps the image, 'according to what is done to savage animals, in order to prevent them to do harm'; turns the epithet into an argument, since Peter 'points out the reason why they slandered, even because they were ignorant of God'; generalises the danger, since at the beginning of the Gospel 'many thought themselves free to live only for themselves'; and gives the definition the tile turns on: 'true liberty, then, is that which harms or injures no one.'

Clarke renders the verb 'to muzzle, i.e., stop their mouths, leave them nothing to say; let them assert, but ever be unable to bring proof', says flatly that the Jews 'used their liberty for a cloak of maliciousness — for a pretext of rebellion', and limits the honour to 'whom honour is due'. Wesley breaks with the prevailing tone entirely: the ignorance is that 'of them who blame you, because they do not know you: a strong motive to pity them', and he grounds the universal honour in three facts, that all men are 'made in the image of God, bought by his Son, and designed for his kingdom'.

debates.question: How should the ignorance of the accusers be regarded?

positions.view: With contempt: the muzzling implies 'there is something of the animal about these foolish men'.
With pity: it is the ignorance 'of them who blame you, because they do not know you: a strong motive to pity them'.
Between the two: malice may be at the bottom, but 'the charges were really based on ignorance'.

debates.question: How far does 'honour all men' reach?

positions.view: It is qualified — 'not with the same honour' — being respect due 'according to their personal worth, and to the rank and office which they sustain'.
It is universal: 'there is not one who can be entirely despised, not one who has quite lost the likeness of Christ', and 'none are to be neglected'.

outliers.view: Alone answers the slander with pity rather than contempt, and grounds universal honour in creation, redemption and destiny.
Reads the whole verse as a reply to the charge that the Church was a subversive body claiming to stand above the laws.

themes: For so is the will of God, that with well doing ye may put to silence the ignorance of foolish men:
As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God.
Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.

18.pericope_label: Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear; not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward

schools.summary: Ellicott says the word 'brings forward the family or household relation of servant or slave to master, and not... the mere fact of ownership', and answers the objection that such directions are odd in a letter to Jewish Christians: 'there were large numbers of Hebrews in this position.' On the fear he insists 'all implies everything which goes to make up true fear', meaning no 'unmanly cowardice'; and on 'thankworthy' he reports that 'some of the older Roman Catholic divines pressed it into the service of the supererogation theory', reading it as 'this deserves grace as its reward', which he dismisses — 'it is needless to point out how shallow a view of duty is implied in the thought that it was more than duty to be thus submissive.' Barnes presses the word into a denial, since it 'should not and cannot be employed to prove that slavery existed in the churches to which Peter wrote, and still less to prove that he approved of slavery', and rules out the obvious English of the next phrase: it 'does not mean that it was worthy of thanks, or that God would thank them for doing it... but that such conduct would meet with his approbation'. Robertson glosses the noun 'house servants (slaves) in distinction from the general term' for slave, objects that 'acceptable calls for' a different Greek word, and states the condition exactly: 'suffering is not a blessing in and of itself, but, if one's duty to God is involved, then one can meet it with gladness of heart.'

Gill supplies the objection Peter answers, and it is doctrinal rather than social: the Jews held 'that because they were the seed of Abraham, they ought not to be the servants of any', and believers among them thought they need not serve unbelieving masters, 'nor indeed believing ones, because they were equally brethren in Christ'. Calvin explains the choice of word by exposure, domestics having 'came more in contact with their masters, and were more liable to be ill-treated'; defines the fear by its opposites, as 'that sincere and willing reverence, which they acknowledge by their office to be due', set against dissimulation and forced subjection, concluding that 'fear arises from a right knowledge of duty'; takes the next word as praise; and notes why the assurance was needed, since 'the condition of servants was very hard: they were counted no better than cattle. Such indignity might have driven them to despair.'

Clarke glosses the froward master as 'the crooked, perverse, unreasonable morose, and austere', and divides responsibility: 'your time belongs to your master; obey him in every thing that is not sinful; if he employs you about unreasonable or foolish things, let him answer for it. He may waste your time... you can only fill up your time.' Following Macknight he finds a principle in such obedience: obligations depend not 'on the character of the person' served 'but on the unalterable relations of things established by God'. Wesley makes the fear double: fear 'of offending them or God'.

Henry states the fact plainly — 'servants in those days generally were slaves, and had heathen masters, who often used them cruelly' — and the principle as a rule: 'the sinful misconduct of one relation, does not justify sinful behaviour in the other', adding, against the drift of the passage, that 'masters should be meek and gentle'.

debates.question: Does the word Peter uses settle whether slavery existed in these churches?

positions.view: No. It 'should not and cannot be employed to prove that slavery existed in the churches to which Peter wrote, and still less to prove that he approved of slavery', applying equally to hired domestics.
They generally were slaves: 'servants in those days generally were slaves, and had heathen masters, who often used them cruelly.'
The word settles a different question — it marks the household relation rather than 'the mere fact of ownership'.

debates.question: What does 'this is thankworthy' mean?

positions.view: Not that submission earns grace, as 'some of the older Roman Catholic divines' held in 'the service of the supererogation theory'.
That such conduct 'would meet with his approbation' — the word meaning praise or acceptance, not thanks owed.
'Acceptable' is the wrong English, since it 'calls for' a different Greek word; the point is that suffering counts only when 'one's duty to God is involved'.

outliers.view: Divides responsibility between master and servant by the clock: the master may waste the servant's time and 'play the fool with his own property; you can only fill up your time'.
Turns the exhortation back on the masters, adding against the drift of the passage that they 'should be meek and gentle'.

themes: Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear; not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward.
For this is thankworthy, if a man for conscience toward God endure grief, suffering wrongfully.

20.pericope_label: For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example

schools.summary: Ellicott hears the opening question as a joke: the noun is 'a poetical and pagan-sounding word, not elsewhere found in the New Testament', so 'the sense may be said to be slightly humorous' — 'if you make a blunder (such is the meaning of fault here — it might include such things as the breaking of dishes), and receive a buffet for it (or a box on the ear — a common punishment of slaves for trifling faults), and bear it with fortitude, do you expect to be made the subject of an heroic or dithyrambic poem?' He objects that 'the translators have limited St. Peter's meaning by the insertion of the last two words', takes the calling back to Paul's practice of forewarning 'of the tribulations attending all who wished to enter the kingdom of God', and finds a premise hidden in the connective, 'that Christ's experience must needs be that of every Christian'. Robertson catches the same register — 'what price glory?' — with the moral, 'no posing as a martyr allowed here'; notes there is 'no for it in the Greek here'; says they were called 'to suffer without flinching'; and traces the word for example to Clement of Alexandria's use of it 'of the copy-head at the top of a child's exercise book'. Barnes glosses the buffeting as striking 'with the fist', imagines servants 'struck in sudden anger, either by the hand, or by anything that was accessible', calls the example 'a writing copy, such as is set for children; or an outline or sketch for a painter to fill up', and cautions that Peter 'does not say that this was the only object for which Christ suffered'.

Calvin raises the objection the verse invites: when God punishes our sins, 'patience is certainly a sacrifice of sweet odour to him', so how can Peter deny it glory? His answer is that 'Peter does not here speak simply but comparatively; for it is a small and slender praise to bear with submission a just punishment, in comparison with that of an innocent man, who willingly bears the wrongs of men, only because he fears God.' He also refuses to keep the passage among the servants, since it 'ought not to be confined to that subject', and finds the consolation comparative: 'nothing seems more unworthy, and therefore less tolerable, than undeservedly to suffer; but when we turn our eyes to the Son of God, this bitterness is mitigated.'

Clarke reads the buffeting historically rather than domestically: the Christian slaves 'were buffeted because they were Christians, and because they would not join with their masters in idolatrous worship' — not for blunders. He also reports the textual variant, that 'many MSS. and most of the versions' read 'for you' rather than 'for us', a reading 'which I think is genuine', and puts the calling bluntly: 'ye cannot expect to fare better than your master.'

debates.question: Why were the servants buffeted?

positions.view: For trifling faults — 'it might include such things as the breaking of dishes' — a box on the ear being 'a common punishment of slaves for trifling faults'.
For their religion: they 'were buffeted because they were Christians, and because they would not join with their masters in idolatrous worship'.

debates.question: Is patience under deserved punishment worth nothing?

positions.view: Not nothing, but little by comparison: 'Peter does not here speak simply but comparatively', since patience under just punishment is 'a small and slender praise' beside innocent suffering.
It earns no glory at all: 'no posing as a martyr allowed here.'

outliers.view: Reads the opening question as deliberate humour, paraphrasing it as an offer of a dithyrambic poem for bearing a box on the ear.
Traces the word for example to the copy-head at the top of a child's exercise book, 'including all the letters of the alphabet'.

themes: For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God.
For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps:

22.pericope_label: Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth: who, when he was reviled, reviled not again

schools.summary: Ellicott insists the verse be read forward: 'it is not the sinlessness of Christ by itself that is here set as an example before the servants, but His sinlessness in combination with His ill-treatment, or rather, His meekness under the combination.' He notices a substitution in the quotation, Isaiah's word being 'one of violent transgression' where Peter uses the mild word he had just applied to a servant's blunder, so the sense is 'who never made a fault — such as household servants were often committing', the second clause referring to 'petty acts of dishonesty, and petty deceits to screen themselves from punishment'. He then returns the scene to the servants' quarters, where 'instances are not wanting in the comic poets where they lose their self-control' under reviling, while bodily maltreatment left them only 'threats of what they would do — run away, or burn the house, or poison the food'. Barnes lists the charges — 'accused of being a seditious man; spoken of as a deceiver; charged with being in league with Beelzebub' — and adds the double duty: 'it is as much our duty to live so as not to deserve the reproaches of others, as it is to bear them with patience.' Robertson reads the verse through its tenses, imperfects 'for repeated incidents', and insists that what was handed over was not another, 'as the Sanhedrin' did, 'but himself'.

Gill states the paradox flatly: Christ 'was in the likeness of sinful flesh', was 'traduced as a sinner by his enemies, and had all the sins of his people on him' — 'but he had no sin in his nature, nor did he commit any in his life' — and traces the restraint case by case, so that on the cross 'he made no return, he opened not his mouth'. Calvin turns the sinlessness against any reader who thinks himself hard done by: 'if any one boasts of his own innocence, he must know that Christ did not suffer as a malefactor', and since James makes the man who offends not in his tongue perfect, 'no one of us can dare claim' it. He keeps the received text of the last clause and finds consolation in it, that those who 'patiently endured the reproaches and violence of the wicked' should know 'they would have God as their defender'.

Clarke explains the guile independently of Ellicott: it is mentioned 'because those who do wrong generally strive to screen themselves by prevarication and lies'. He also reports a variant that changes the sentence, the Vulgate and some Latin fathers reading 'he delivered himself to him who judged unrighteously', meaning Pilate — 'some critics approve of this reading, but it has not sufficient evidence to recommend it as genuine.' Wesley makes the pairing occupational: the example 'is peculiarly adapted to the state of servants, who easily slide either into sin or guile, reviling their fellowservants, or threatening them — the natural result of anger without power'.

Cyril of Jerusalem turns the verses into a list of charges Christ could not have faced: he was not led to death 'for covetousness, since He was a Teacher of poverty'; 'not for smiting or striking hastily, for He turned the other cheek also to the smiter; not for despising the Law, for He was the fulfiller of the Law; not for reviling a prophet, for it was Himself who was proclaimed by the Prophets' — then quotes this passage entire, ending 'who came to His passion, not unwillingly, but willing'.

debates.question: Why is guile named alongside sin?

positions.view: Because it was the characteristic servant's fault: 'petty acts of dishonesty, and petty deceits to screen themselves from punishment', since 'those who do wrong generally strive to screen themselves by prevarication and lies'.

debates.question: To whom did Christ commit himself?

positions.view: To the Father who judges righteously — and it was himself he handed over, not another 'as the Sanhedrin' did.
Reports, without endorsing, a Latin reading in which 'he delivered himself to him who judged unrighteously', meaning Pilate.

outliers.view: Reconstructs the servants' side of the quarrel from the comic poets, and lists what slaves threatened when they could not strike back — 'run away, or burn the house, or poison the food'.
Uses the verses as a forensic acquittal, enumerating the crimes for which Christ demonstrably was not condemned.

themes: Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth:
Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:

24.pericope_label: Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree... by whose stripes ye were healed

schools.summary: Ellicott denies that the verse continues the argument from example: it 'is intended to make the readers feel the claims of gratitude, not to set before them another point in which Christ was to be imitated' — though it still reinforces the earlier points, Christ suffering 'in His own body, so that He could sympathise with the corporal chastisements of these poor servants; and on the tree, too, the wicked slave's death'. On the preposition he reports that 'most modern scholars are agreed to reject on the tree, in favour of the marginal to', the sense being what colloquial English calls 'on-to the tree'. Barnes takes the phrase sacrificially — 'he did not make expiation by offering a bloody victim, but was himself the sacrifice' — and argues from an impossibility to a substitution: it 'cannot mean that Christ so took upon himself the sins of men as to become himself a sinner', so 'he was treated as if he had been a sinner, in order that we might be treated as if we had not sinned'. Robertson supplies the verb, the common word 'of bringing sacrifice to the altar', with Bigg's 'here St. Peter puts the Cross in the place of the altar', and traces the noun, 'originally just wood, then something made of wood, as a gibbet or cross'.

Gill takes the load at its widest: Christ bore 'all sorts of sin, original and actual', and 'all that is in sin... the demerit of it, as both filth, guilt, and punishment'. Calvin numbers what the verse does, against reading it as example only, which 'would have been very frigid': 'that Christ by his death has given us an example of patience'; 'that by his death he restored us to life'; and 'that we, being dead to sins, ought to live to righteousness'. He keeps the sacrificial frame: 'as under the Law, the sinner, that he might be released from guilt, substituted a victim in his own place; so Christ took on himself the curse due to our sins.'

Clarke answers an ancient error first — 'his own self' means 'not another in his place, as some anciently supposed, because they thought it impossible that the Christ should suffer' — then states the negative violently: Christ 'bore the punishment due to our sins. In no other sense could Christ bear them. To say that they were so imputed to him as if they had been his own, and that the Father beheld him as blackened with imputed sin, is monstrous, if not blasphemous.' He renders the participle 'being freed from sin — delivered out of its power', so 'that righteousness should be our master now, as sin was before', and keeps the healing in the register of the stripes. Wesley agrees in a phrase — 'that is, the punishment due to them' — and closes with a count: righteousness 'is one only. The sins we had committed, and he bore, were manifold.'

Cyril of Jerusalem sets the transaction as a dilemma resolved: 'either that God, in His truth, should destroy all men, or that in His loving-kindness He should cancel the sentence. But behold the wisdom of God; He preserved both the truth of His sentence, and the exercise of His loving-kindness.'

debates.question: In what sense did Christ bear our sins?

positions.view: Only in the sense of bearing the punishment. To say they were imputed to him 'as if they had been his own, and that the Father beheld him as blackened with imputed sin, is monstrous, if not blasphemous'.
By substitution rather than transfer: 'he was treated as if he had been a sinner, in order that we might be treated as if we had not sinned.'
At the widest: 'all that is in sin... the demerit of it, as both filth, guilt, and punishment.'
Sacrificially, as the victim substituted under the Law: 'Christ took on himself the curse due to our sins.'

debates.question: Is this verse example or atonement?

positions.view: Neither wholly: it is 'intended to make the readers feel the claims of gratitude, not to set before them another point in which Christ was to be imitated'.
Both, and more: example alone 'would have been very frigid', so the verse also says that by his death 'he restored us to life'.

outliers.view: Calls the doctrine that the Father beheld Christ as blackened with imputed sin 'monstrous, if not blasphemous'.
Hears in 'on the tree' the slave's own manner of death, so that the atonement is described in terms the servants addressed would feel.

themes: Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.

25.pericope_label: For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls

schools.summary: Ellicott corrects the grammar first — 'the right reading does not attach going astray to sheep, but as predicate of the sentence, ye were going astray like sheep' — and the connective, which explains 'how they came to be in need of healing', paraphrasing the argument: 'Israelites though you are, your consciences and memories tell you that you were as far gone in wilful error as any Gentiles.' He then admits a defect and excuses it: 'the two metaphors, of healing and going astray, do not match very well, but the fact that both are quotations from Isaiah makes their disagreement less harsh.' On the tense of the return he is precise, the verb pointing 'to the actual historical time at which it took place, rather than the position now occupied'. Barnes keeps the figure descriptive — 'we were like a flock without a shepherd... without a protector, and were exposed to every kind of danger' — and glosses the second title 'overseer', a word for anyone who 'inspects or oversees anything, as public works, or the execution of treaties'. Robertson observes that this is the only place where Christ is so called, that 'Philo calls God' by the same word, and that both titles are combined in Ezekiel.

Gill treats the title 'sheep' as a problem rather than a compliment: God's elect are sheep before conversion 'not that they have the agreeable properties of sheep, as to be meek, harmless, innocent, clean, and profitable, for they are the reverse of all this', nor because they are 'unprejudiced against, and predisposed unto the Gospel' — they are sheep 'in electing grace', by the Father's gift. Calvin locates the emphasis elsewhere: on the word 'sheep' 'there is no particular stress', the weight falling on 'that every one had turned to his own way', so that 'we are all going astray from the way of salvation, and proceeding in the way of ruin, until Christ brings us back'; and he concludes that 'all who are not ruled by Christ, are wandering like lost sheep in the ways of error', by which 'is condemned the whole wisdom of the world'.

Clarke turns the point on the readers' situation: they 'were not in a better moral condition than your oppressors', until Christ 'called you back from your wanderings, by sending you the Gospel of his grace'. On the second title he insists on the translation and its consequence: unless the English word is understood as the Greek overseer 'it can convey to us no meaning of the original', and since Christ 'is still supreme Bishop or Overseer in his Church' he alone is 'Episcopus episcoporum, the Bishop of bishops; a title which the Romish pontiffs have blasphemously usurped'. Wesley calls him 'the kind observer, inspector, or overseer of your souls'.

debates.question: In what sense were they sheep before conversion?

positions.view: Only in electing grace and the Father's gift — not for any sheep-like properties, since 'they are the reverse of all this'.
Descriptively: 'we were like a flock without a shepherd... without a protector, and were exposed to every kind of danger.'
The word carries no particular stress at all; the point is that 'every one had turned to his own way'.

outliers.view: Uses the title 'Bishop of your souls' polemically, since Christ alone is 'Episcopus episcoporum, the Bishop of bishops; a title which the Romish pontiffs have blasphemously usurped'.
Concedes that Peter's two metaphors 'do not match very well', excusing the mixture only because both are quotations from the same prophecy.

themes: For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.
